name: Laws of Indices
description: Use the core exponent laws confidently when multiplying, dividing, and raising powers.
script_scope: Teach the meaning of a base and an index/exponent with small whole-number examples, then teach the six laws of indices listed in the chapter: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n); a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n); (a^m)^n = a^(mn); (ab)^n = a^n b^n; (a/b)^n = a^n/b^n; and a^0 = 1 as used by the book. Show why each law works through repeated multiplication before using it as a shortcut. Include simplification of products and quotients with the same base, powers of powers, powers of products/quotients, and short mixed expressions. A learner should be able to choose the correct law, keep the base unchanged when appropriate, combine exponents correctly, and check an answer by expanding a small example. Keep fractional, negative, and decimal indices for the next subtopic.

name: Fractional, Negative and Decimal Indices
description: Read fractional powers as roots, negative powers as reciprocals, and decimal powers as fractions.
script_scope: Teach a^(1/n) as the nth root of a and a^(m/n) as an nth root combined with the mth power, matching the chapter's index/surd laws. Teach a negative index as a reciprocal, including negative fractional indices, and convert terminating decimal exponents such as 0.5, 0.25, 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6 into simple fractions before evaluating. Use perfect powers so the learner can see exact results, and include decimal bases such as 0.2 or 0.4 where the chapter rewrites one decimal as a power of another. Explain the order of operations: first understand the positive fractional power, then take the reciprocal when the exponent is negative. A learner should be able to evaluate supported fractional/negative/decimal powers exactly and avoid the common error of making the base negative when only the exponent is negative.

name: Common Bases and Missing Exponents
description: Rewrite powers with a common base so missing exponents and compact expressions become easy to solve.
script_scope: Teach the chapter's central simplification habit of rewriting quantities with a common base before combining exponents. Cover equivalent forms such as 64 = 2^6, 8 = 2^3, 81 = 3^4, 27 = 3^3, and decimal relations such as 0.04 = (0.2)^2 and 0.008 = (0.2)^3. Use these rewrites to simplify products/quotients, solve equations where both sides can be expressed with the same base, and determine a missing exponent represented by a question mark. Include powers of 10 and simple scientific-notation style expressions as they appear in the objective section. A learner should be able to choose a useful common base, translate every factor into that base, combine indices, equate exponents when the bases match, and check the result by substitution. Keep sums/differences of powers that require factoring for the next subtopic.

name: Exponential Equations by Factoring Powers
description: Solve sums and differences of powers by taking out a common exponential factor.
script_scope: Teach how to solve equations containing sums or differences such as 2^(x-1) + 2^(x+1) by factoring out the smaller common power, exactly as the chapter does in solved and objective problems. Show the same idea with coefficients, rewritten bases such as 4^x = 2^(2x), and equations where a reciprocal base must be rewritten with a negative exponent before comparing indices. Emphasize that a^p + a^q is not a^(p+q); addition requires factoring, while multiplication allows exponent addition. A learner should be able to identify the common power, factor it, simplify the ordinary numerical factor, rewrite the remaining equation to a common base, and solve the exponent. Include fresh practice on both sums and differences and a capstone that mixes a base rewrite with common-factor extraction.

name: Linked and Multi-Base Exponent Relations
description: Handle exponent problems where several bases or variables are linked by equalities.
script_scope: Teach the relational exponent patterns demonstrated in the chapter: converting a product such as 8^x·2^y into one base; solving two linear equations that arise from exponent comparison; cyclic relations such as x = y^a, y = z^b, z = x^c leading to abc = 1; equal-power chains such as 2^x = 4^y = 8^z; and the chapter pattern 2^x = 3^y = 6^(-z), which yields a reciprocal-exponent relation because 2×3=6. Also cover short chained-base relations where substitutions collapse intermediate bases. A learner should be able to replace each exponential statement with a simpler exponent relation, solve the resulting ordinary equations, and recognise when exponents cancel around a cycle. Do not introduce logarithms as a new method.

name: Surd Meaning, Order and Laws
description: Understand what a surd is, identify its order, and simplify roots using the chapter's surd laws.
script_scope: Teach the book's definition of a surd: an nth root of a rational number that is irrational, with n as the order. Distinguish a true surd such as √7 from a root that simplifies to a rational number such as √9. Teach the laws listed in the chapter: nth-root notation as a fractional index, root of a product, root of a quotient, raising an nth root to the nth power, nested root order multiplication, and powers of roots. Use these laws to multiply/divide simple surds and to extract perfect factors, for example √72 = 6√2. A learner should be able to identify the order of a surd, decide whether a displayed root is actually irrational, simplify products/quotients of roots, and pull perfect square/cube factors out correctly. Keep comparison of different-order surds and special perfect-square surd forms for later subtopics.

name: Comparing Surds of Different Orders
description: Compare positive surds by converting them to a common order and then comparing radicands.
script_scope: Teach the comparison method used in the chapter's solved example: note the orders of the positive surds, take the L.C.M. of those orders, rewrite every surd with that common order, and compare the resulting positive radicands. Begin with same-order roots, then compare two roots of different orders, and finally compare three or more values such as square, cube and fourth roots. Include finite objective-style comparisons involving expressions like 2^(1/2), 3^(1/3), and 4^(1/4) by converting them to a common denominator/order; do not introduce an unsupported general theorem about n^(1/n). A learner should be able to convert positive surds to one common order without changing their values, compare exactly without decimal approximation, and identify the greatest or least option.

name: Perfect-Square Surds and Nested Square Roots
description: Recognize expressions such as a ± 2√b as perfect squares and simplify nested square roots.
script_scope: Teach the perfect-square structure used repeatedly in the chapter: (√m + √n)^2 = m + n + 2√(mn) and (√m - √n)^2 = m + n - 2√(mn). Show how to match a nested expression such as √(5 + 2√6) by finding m and n with m+n = 5 and mn = 6, then taking the positive square root. Cover both plus and minus forms, expressions such as √(8 - 2√15), and sums/differences of paired nested roots where opposite surd parts cancel. Explain sign choice carefully: the principal square root is non-negative. A learner should be able to recognize the hidden square, identify the two component radicands, simplify the outer square root, and combine paired nested roots without losing a sign.

name: Reciprocal Surd Pairs and x ± 1/x
description: Use opposite-sign surd pairs to simplify reciprocals and expressions involving x and 1/x.
script_scope: Build from the chapter's use of opposite-sign pairs such as (3 + 2√2)(3 - 2√2) = 1. Show that when the product is 1, the opposite-sign partner is the reciprocal, so 1/(3 + 2√2) = 3 - 2√2. Use this to simplify x + 1/x, x - 1/x, and their squared consequences x^2 + 1/x^2, as well as the chapter-style expressions involving √x and 1/√x when x itself is a perfect-square surd. Explain that the paired multiplication is a difference of squares and avoid presenting a broad rationalisation syllabus beyond the transformations actually used in this chapter. A learner should be able to verify the reciprocal by multiplication, cancel surd parts correctly, and derive squared expressions from a known sum or difference.

name: Integrated Surd and Index Identities
description: Combine the chapter's index laws, algebraic identities, cube-root patterns, and factor-count ideas in harder problems.
script_scope: Use this as a capstone for the less direct objective patterns in the chapter. Teach the factor identity (x-1)(x^3+x^2+x+1)=x^4-1 as the structure behind a solved example with a fractional index; the cube expansion relation (u+v)^3 = u^3+v^3+3uv(u+v) for paired cube roots; cancellation of exponents in cyclic products; counting prime factors with multiplicity after rewriting powered integers into prime powers; and repeated difference-of-squares products such as (a-1)(a+1)(a^2+1)... . Keep every method traceable to the chapter's solved examples or objective questions. A learner should be able to spot the useful structure before calculating, reduce a long expression through identities, and combine two or more earlier surd/index skills without resorting to unsupported shortcuts.
